title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword
description:
Fight through bloodstained battlefields of intense swordplay action. Explore the historic Japanese capital of Edo-era Kyoto, twisted by malevolent clouds of Malice. With every stage cloaked in mystery, danger and intrigue. Battle against monstrosities from the underworld known as Genma in a tale of dark fantasy.

Follow the tale of a samurai who wields the Oni Gauntlet, a mystical artifact that grants its bearer the power to slay Genma.

Through gritty, blood-soaked brawls, he searches for his reason to fight. What fate awaits at the end of his path?

critic_reviews.quote: Onimusha: Way of the Sword is easily a contender for game of the year, as it blends merciless action with skill-based combat in a near-seamless way. The story and visuals complement the ridiculously sharp gameplay extremely well, and though the camera can be a little problematic on rare occasions, that shouldn’t stop you from experiencing Capcom’s latest banger.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a visually stunning revival that successfully brings Capcom’s classic franchise into the modern era using the RE Engine. Musashi injects a refreshing sense of personality into dark fantasy Kyoto, especially during the game’s intense and cinematic boss fights. This is definitely an action adventure game of the year contender.
As rewarding as it is difficult, Onimusha isn’t just one of the best games of the year; it’s one of the best action games ever made.

For as long as I can remember, I have wanted to be perfect for 10 seconds. Onimusha: Way of the Sword understands that desire. Each time I landed a perfectly timed Issen, pulled off a risky deflect, or landed a combo at just the right time, I felt like I had accomplished something. I had put myself to the test, and I’d succeeded. It’s a testament to Way of the Sword’s combat that I could beat it without using some of the systems designed to help you progress – not because you don’t need them, but because it leaves room for you to truly understand its action and overcome their absence through sheer determination. Even if I hadn’t intentionally made things harder for myself, though, I still would have loved spending time with Okuni, Takamura, Murasaki, Shizuka, and nearly all the denizens of this world. I still would have thought that Musashi himself is one of the coolest, most interesting protagonists in any video game, and I would have loved going on this journey with him. I still would have savored the creative fights against Ganryu and Benkei and a dozen others I won’t spoil here. My journey reflected Musashi's, and Onimusha made that possible. The best part of life is the challenge. You have to learn to love the fight.

Onimusha is a criminally underrated series, and while it was not a series I was expecting to be revived, I am delighted to see it make a comeback. And with the sheer quality that Capcom has pumped into Way of the Sword, I have no doubt that this is a game that is going to sell like hotcakes, and I'm already getting my hopes up for another new Onimusha title, In a competitive field, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is hands-down the best action-adventure title of the year so far. Its combat system is as electrifying as it is challenging to master, and it's backed up by a great story and characters, and a lovely little world to explore. Capcom can probably scarcely believe how well its 2026 is going. Here's hoping its new golden age continues for many years to come.

Onimusha is back and ready to claim the highest honors. Content,
quality, fun – the full package is right here.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a triumphant return for Capcom’s samurai action series, combining spectacular visuals with deep, demanding combat built around precise parries, the classic Issen technique, and a varied arsenal of Oni weapons. Strong performances, memorable boss battles, rewarding progression, and an excellent recreation of feudal Japan make it one of Capcom’s most accomplished action games, while repetitive sub-bosses and a few minor presentation issues do little to diminish an outstanding experience.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword proves Capcom can't go wrong in 2026, offering combat that stands out with every swing of the blade and fascinating characters.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword masterfully revives the franchise with gameplay rich in mechanics and variety, full of boss battles that could make even FromSoftware fans envious. The story is like an incredible shonen anime. Musashi is a captivating and funny protagonist, accompanied by a cast of equally interesting supporting characters and antagonists who come together to create one of the best journeys Capcom has ever crafted.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is such a refreshing action game, with focus on its combat systems and cinematic narrative. In those respects, it sets a high standard for all other video games. The only critiques some could make is that it’s a very linear game, and that could be a problem for some. It’s also maybe 20 hours long, and once the story’s finished, there isn’t a breadth of post-game modes. Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a cinematic action game, and Capcom exceeded any expectations people could have in that regard. It just lacks some kind of score mode, or Bloody Palace to keep players invested beyond the main story. I loved Onimusha: Way of the Sword, and I think it will be celebrated as a modern action classic.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is not just the best possible comeback for a franchise that hadn't seen a new installment in 20 years; it is the starting point for what could become Capcom's most epic IP of the coming decade. The game has it all: spectacular combat, incredible graphics and animations, and a magnificent story driven by unforgettable characters.
Some writing and delivery issues are about the only flaws present in an otherwise incredible Onimusha experience. Capcom’s rich vein of form continues.

Despite some repetition, an overlong finale and an occasionally frustrating camera, Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers a remarkable experience. Its highly addictive gameplay, rewarding progression, striking atmosphere and Musashi’s incredible charisma make this long-awaited comeback a resounding success.
The way of the samurai shines bright in Onimusha: Way of the Sword, marking a triumphant return for Capcom's long-running action RPG series.
A stylish title with incredible combat, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is easily one of the best action-adventure titles of the year and one that you shouldn't miss.

With Onimusha: The Way of the Sword Capcom doesn't seem to have wanted to completely reinvent the franchise. Instead, it took what made the retro games special and combined it with a more modern combat system, spectacular presentation, and some ideas that bring the experience closer to the Soulslike genre. Way of the Sword stands out as one of the most interesting revivals of a classic franchise and continues to mark one of Capcom’s best years.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a successful return for the legendary series, one that wisely steers clear of the current trend of turning action games into ‘soulslikes’. The game shines with its brilliant, gory combat system, exemplary Sekiro-esque parrying, charismatic characters (the superbly animated Musashi!) and fantastic bosses. It retains the series’ atmosphere and beautiful visuals, and the optimisation for the PS5 is flawless. The overly passive common enemies are a slight disappointment, and unfortunately there aren’t enough interesting puzzles; even so, it remains a highly satisfying power fantasy and a wonderful tribute to the series’ entire legacy.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a triumphant revival that rewards patience with exceptional combat, demanding boss fights, and surprisingly strong level design. Its slow narrative buildup and uneven side content hold it back, but once its systems fully open up, Capcom delivers a deeply satisfying action game worthy of the Onimusha name.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic return for one of the most promising franchises in the entire industry. With an excellent story and exceptional combat, Capcom hits the mark once again, delivering a title that is a true spectacle. Capturing the best of its blend of samurai and horror, it transforms into an exciting and action-packed experience that should be remembered as one of the best of the year.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword brings the samurai saga back in full force, delivering a distinctive combat system alongside challenging and memorable boss encounters. Its highly polished execution makes it a strong return for the franchise, offering an experience that welcomes longtime fans and newcomers alike.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an often outstanding action game that bears all the hallmarks of a modern Capcom masterpiece. Its combat is clearly the main draw and it's a superb system once it gets rolling. The boss fights in particular are some of the best you'll find on PS5. But even beyond the sword-swinging skirmishes, Way of the Sword impresses with great characters and eye-popping cutscenes. This is a fantastic revival of a franchise that's been sleeping for far too long.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a welcome return for the series, and Capcom has been doing an incredible job with the action genre this year.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a successful return for a series that had been absent for far too long. The combat system—precise and heavily reliant on timing—is undoubtedly the highlight of this new entry in the Capcom franchise, while the atmosphere of a Kyoto overrun by the Genma miasma creates truly evocative moments. Although some limitations regarding side activities and a degree of repetition prevent the adventure from achieving true excellence, Musashi and his journey amidst samurai and demons still manage to leave a lasting impression. It is a compact, spectacular experience that remains, above all, faithful to the spirit of the Onimusha franchise.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword’s cast, quest, numerous asides, and the evolution of techniques and combat throughout this adventure have the weight and depth to make you roar in triumph, groan in agony, and hit most of the feelings in between along the way. And that’s exactly what I want out of my demon-slaying samurai action-adventure.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic return for a franchise many thought Capcom had left behind. Even when I thought combat had hit its peak, the game kept layering on deeper mechanics, richer upgrades, and thrilling boss encounters that demand your absolute best. In a stacked month of massive releases, Musashi’s journey isn't just worth your time—it's an absolute must-play for action fans.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword may be the best game in the series and by quite a large margin. Definitely start out on Story difficulty to find your feet and get used to the game’s pacing of enemy attacks, but once you’re in the zone, it is a genuinely wonderful game from start to finish.

It is the best comeback we could have dreamed of for the series after 20 years of silence. Onimusha: Way of the Sword won us over, despite initial reservations and the occasional hiccup along the journey—inevitable given its generous length. It delivers pure, unadulterated action without trying to turn the franchise into something it isn't, offering a truly grand adventure packed with memorable characters, formidable bosses, and a magnificent setting. One could hardly ask for more from a Capcom currently firing on all cylinders and racking up serious Game of the Year contenders... Except, perhaps, that they treat *Dino Crisis* with the same affection they are now showing Onimusha.

After a 20-year wait, Onimusha returns in spectacular fashion. Way of the Sword delivers a fantastic combat system, stunning visuals, and a compelling story that welcomes both veterans and newcomers, making it easily one of the best action games of the year.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks the triumphant return of Capcom’s classic franchise. With fluid, beautifully choreographed combat, charismatic characters, creative bosses, and spectacular art direction, the game modernizes the series without losing its essence. Its low difficulty and less-inspired side content are minor flaws in an otherwise exceptional adventure.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword finally ends the 20-year wait. The thrilling samurai fights we've been looking for, combined with a fun and engaging story, are now livening up our PlayStation 5 console.

Amid a sea of mediocre Soulslikes, Onimusha: Way of the Sword arrives as a much-needed breath of fresh air. Capcom has delivered a top-tier action title with remarkable depth and variety, keeping you fully engaged from start to finish. While a few minor flaws exist, they do little to dull the game's overall excellence. It is a triumphant comeback for the series, positioning Onimusha to reclaim its spot as a dominant force in the action genre.
A fantastically self-assured reboot of Onimusha, which is significantly better than any of the previous games, with excellent combat, plenty to see and do, and some engaging storytelling.

Capcom’s willingness to return to old franchises is continuing to pay off, because Onimusha: Way of the Sword is yet another banger from a developer that just cannot stop winning. It’s easily the best game that it’s released this year, which includes behemoths like Resident Evil Requiem and Pragmata, and if you’re an Onimusha fan praying that this new game will finally revive the series, you should be very excited about the future. Now do Dino Crisis next, Capcom.

The very identity of Onimusha is back in full force, so it’s time to wipe the grit from your blade and assume the role of a legendary sword savant, comforted in the knowledge that you’re in store for a spellbinding and endlessly rewarding samurai action adventure opus.

Onimusha has repeated boss fights – especially if you complete all of the game’s optional objectives – and that might annoy you if you haven’t dedicated yourself to the Way of the Sword. If you aren’t entering each fight with the intention to do better than before (use fewer heals, take fewer hits), then you’re probably not playing it right. Combat in Onimusha isn’t something to be overcome, but something to savour and improve at, and there’s no way of telling how much better you’ve become without taking on familiar foes.

While you’ll have seen all the various elements of this title in other games before in various forms, Capcom has done a wonderful job bringing it together and forming something that feels relevent and tells a great tale.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword confirms Capcom’s success in masterfully reviving the franchise, pleasing both new and returning fans with its humorous plot, agile combat, and expansive exploration. Although it has its shortcomings—such as excessively tough bosses, limited enemy variety, and minor exploration flaws—these issues do not diminish the brilliance of this excellent title.

The game's linear missions keep the game moving at a solid pace, though the open hub Kyoto area feels out of place and a bit too repetitive. What isn't repetitive, however, is the gameplay, which truly embodies the way of the sword, challenging players to master the katana through an exhilarating combat system built from attacking, parrying, dodging, and breaking enemies. It's all wrapped together in a breathtaking presentation built on the always impressive RE Engine. Capcom walked the way of the sword, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword successfully balances the discipline, strategy, and self-improvement the saying embodies.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a reboot done right. Rather than chase trends, Capcom has updated the gameplay while staying true to its roots. With stellar combat and rewarding exploration, this is one of the best action-adventure games released for the PlayStation 5.

It's hard to imagine how this could be a stronger comeback for Onimusha, and in an already incredible year for Capcom, I can't believe that I'm saying Onimusha: Way of the Sword easily sits at the top of the mountain.

After years of hoping, complaining, and probably bringing up Onimusha more than once when absolutely nobody asked, I can finally say that the series is well and truly back. Way of the Sword feels like a modern version of exactly the kind of game that made me so excited about Onimusha all those years ago.
If you are a fan of titles where combat is the main focus, you definitely have to play this one, as it draws inspiration from the best games on the market while adding its own distinctive touches.

Monsters beware, Musashi is here! One of the best hack and slash titles to come out in some time, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is deliriously fun. When it’s all said and done, Kyoto might be under the scourge of the devilish Genma, but it’s an absolute blast getting lost in it.

Onimusha's return was significant in its own right. But the real value of Way of the Sword lies in the fact that it doesn't simply bring the Onimusha name back. Capcom understood what made the series so beloved and has blended those qualities with the evolution of modern action game design.
With its outstanding sword-fighting action, Onimusha: Way of the Sword scratches at the very edge of the perfect combat system and is already one of the best action games of 2026.

Capcom forges a new katana with Onimusha: Way of the Sword, successfully reinventing the samurai saga for modern times. There is room for improvement, but if this marks the beginning of a second life for the Oni warriors—and we hope it does—it is a great first step along the path of the samurai.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a triumphant return for a series that had been somewhat forgotten by Capcom. Yes, the story is a bit weak, but it inherits the key mechanics that worked for the franchise while introducing interesting gameplay improvements. It is a very entertaining action adventure that offers one of the most satisfying and accessible swordplay experiences in a long time.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a very fun game packed with memorable combat, but the constant reuse of bosses takes a bit of the shine off it, with certain moments in the campaign where the game is simply stalling to make itself seem longer than it needs to be. Even so, it is easily one of the most enjoyable games I played in 2026.
If nothing else, Onimusha: Way of the Sword serves as both a brilliant revitalization of the franchise and an excellent starting point for sequels in the future.

The return of Onimusha coincides with the release of a chapter that looks to the present without forgetting its roots. Way of the Sword undoubtedly modernizes the formula, expands exploration, and builds around Issen a combat system that is as spectacular as it is demanding, one that rewards timing, precision, and a cool head above all. A few shortcomings in the AI and a camera that is not always flawless prevent the game from reaching absolute excellence, but they do not change the bottom line: Capcom has succeeded in bringing one of its most fascinating series back to life without compromising what made it special. And after an absence spanning two console generations, that was by no means a foregone conclusion.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers atmospheric samurai action with a precise, rewarding combat system. Predictable story and recycled bosses hold it back, but it remains a strong modern return to the series.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword's super-fun sword combat really packs a punch and is the star of the show along with the ridiculous game world and cast of characters that'll make things a lot more entertaining if they click with you.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword has one of the best parry systems since Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. Its excellent combat is somewhat marred by an outdated open world and some issues with enemy behavior.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a polished action-adventure with an excellent combat system built around precise parries, dodges and enemy interactions. Its boss fights are particularly impressive, while its small open world and linear levels feel somewhat conservative. The story is serviceable, but the satisfying swordplay, strong visuals and superb Spanish voice acting make it highly recommended.
Sublime swordplay and spectacular samurai horror make Onimusha: Way of the Sword a thrilling return, despite too much repetitive busywork.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an excellent revival of Capcom's samurai series. It's a bit more gritty and nitty but it retains the cheesy humour, too. And while combat is exceptional, not everything clicks in place so seamlessly.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a great modern entry into the long-running and long-dormant Capcom series. The combat and story are great, but open-world bloat makes this Capcom's most divisive release in years.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a great return for the franchise. Musashi is a fantastic new lead, with a supporting cast that shines.

Capcom's Onimusha reboot successfully combines old-school linearity with contemporary melee mechanics. The result is a throwback action-adventure bolstered by ultra-satisfying and modernised combat, as well as some of the most surprisingly unsettling comedy and horror moments in recent memory.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword perhaps doesn't make the best first impression and takes a little time to warm to, but once all of its systems are in play, it becomes pretty enthralling. Ultimately, it's a game worth picking up - even if only for its spectacular, and challenging, boss fights.

user_reviews.author: BeJai
user_reviews.quote:
A challenge without frustration is a hard balance to get right and one that most games fail. Thankfully Onimusha WoTS isn't one of them. 
I am throughly enjoying my playthrough. It has the feeling **** from an older time as far as quest/side quests go but the charm of its characters and the incredibly designed combat more than make up for it. 
Technically speaking I haven't experienced any bugs, crashes or glitches on PS5 Pro. Graphically, while not as impressive as RE: Requiem, the art style and design again make up for what is a minor gripe. 
Capcom are on a roll this year. 3/3 bangers imo.

user_reviews.author: irwanryu
user_reviews.quote: Onimusha: WAY OF THE SWORD​Pros:​Highly addictive combat system: It features five defensive maneuvers: parry, deflect, guard, dodge, and Issen.​Hybrid gameplay: It is not a pure Soulslike, but rather a hack-and-slash game blended with Soulslike mechanics.​Excellent story and memorable characters: Featuring iconic figures like Miyamoto Musashi, Shizuka, and Okuni.​Deep progression and character development: Offers an extensive skill tree, equipment upgrades (swords, armor, and gauntlets), and fantastic character growth for Musashi Miyamoto.​Satisfying combat finishers: A wide variety of boss finishing moves, coupled with incredibly cool Chain Issen or Chain Break Issen mechanics.​Cons:​Repetitive environment: Kyoto City and its missions feel too repetitive and very empty.​Pacing issues: A typical Capcom game trait where the early-to-mid game is rich in missions, but the mid-to-end game feels rushed.​Verdict:For those who enjoy hack-and-slash games with diverse Soulslike mechanics and a great story, I highly recommend this game!

user_reviews.author: treerapol99
user_reviews.quote: After two decades of waiting, Capcom has finally brought back one of its most beloved franchises with Onimusha: Way of the Sword. This isn't just a simple nostalgic cash-grab; it is a complete, ground-up reinvention that successfully modernizes the classic samurai action for a new generation. **Story and Presentation**The game follows the journey of a young, cocky, yet highly skilled Miyamoto Musashi in feudal Kyoto. After acquiring the mysterious Oni Gauntlet, Musashi is thrust into a war against the demonic Genma. The narrative is engaging and well-paced, swapping between different character perspectives to keep the player hooked. What truly elevates the presentation is the outstanding character acting. The facial animations and voice acting are top-notch, perfectly capturing Musashi’s witty, sarcastic charm during intense showdowns. **Gameplay and Combat**Capcom has overhauled the gameplay entirely, abandoning the old tank controls and fixed camera angles in favor of fluid, dynamic movement. The combat feels heavy, deliberate, and incredibly fierce. Every sword strike carries immense weight. While it offers deep mechanical depth reminiscent of games like Nioh, it proudly stays true to its action roots rather than forcing itself into the modern "Soulslike" formula. For players struggling with the difficulty, the inclusion of an optional "Action Prompt" system helps teach defensive and counter-attack windows, making the game accessible without reducing the actual challenge. **Performance**True to Capcom's recent track record, the game runs beautifully. Visually, Kyoto looks stunning, and the performance is incredibly stable on both consoles and PC. Aside from minor frame drops when reloading saves—which are easily fixed—the optimization is practically flawless. **Verdict**Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an outstanding revival that honors its roots while bravely carving out a modern identity. With intense combat, an addictive gameplay loop, and excellent storytelling, Capcom has delivered yet another masterpiece in 2026.

user_reviews.author: BigRunX
user_reviews.quote: The game is absolutely perfect. Musashi is charismatic and likable, and I really love the way his face looks. The gameplay is excellent, adding new elements to the classic games while still keeping the essence of what made them great. The story is fantastic too.Easily a 10/10. I want more games like this! Not everything needs to be open-world or Soulslike. Onimusha is living proof of that.

user_reviews.author: VastoLord_3
user_reviews.quote: Cortar e fatiar que jogabilidade gostosa, só joguem e aproveitem. Aliás joguem no modo carnificina

user_reviews.author: Lonejumper23
user_reviews.quote: This is the first game I have played that runs at 120 Hz, 60 FPS, Performance Mode and Ray Tracing on the PS5 Pro. This is just amazing to see a game play and look like this everyone! This is how games should look on this generation’s hardware. I am having so much fun diving down the rabbit hole this story is telling and it’s on a different level. I highly recommend paying the money for this game and having a gaming experience like this. Capcom is nailing it out of the park this year and this game could be GOY easily. It’s going to win awards.

user_reviews.author: Solidops
user_reviews.quote: this is pure fan service. fun exploration. fun boss fights and really fun combat. the parry system is by far my fav way to cut down enemies. kyoto is fun to explore and hides treasures everywhere. just a fun time while playing. if your not a fan of the series and thinking this is a souls like then your not going to like it but if you have played the old ones this is a refreshing way to bring back the series.

user_reviews.author: WheatWarrior
user_reviews.quote:
There are only a handful of times when a modern entry of an older game manages to surpass the original, and this Onimusha is a perfect example. It’s genuinely a work of art. It keeps the classic feel that made the original special while seamlessly introducing modern gameplay elements that fit perfectly.

Everything flows incredibly well. Even after losing to a boss multiple times, I never once felt like the game was being unfair. In fact, every retry felt rewarding because I learned something new—whether it was recognizing an animation, understanding an attack pattern, or figuring out the right moment to strike.

It's a meticulously crafted and curated game, from combat to pacing and enemy design. It’s the kind of game that respects its roots while understanding exactly where modern design can make the experience even better.

user_reviews.author: el_ramon
user_reviews.quote: In a way, the game is a typical old school Onimusha with a partially open main map and other smaller, linear levels. While the game doesn't offer anything particularly special, it's a lot of fun. Regular enemies are easy to defeat, but after a few hours, bosses appear that aren't so easy. You have to adjust your fighting style from time to time. The story is also well written and well told.

user_reviews.author: MagmaCanon
user_reviews.quote:
Unglaublich Capcom hat in nur einem Jahr 4 Spiele raus gebracht und sie sind alle Bangers, da zählt auch Onimusha: Way of the Sword natürlich mit dazu.
Es hat hier und da seine Schwächen wie das die Gegener nicht aggressive genug sind (sie greifen nicht häufig an, oder brauchen viel zu lange).
Obwohl ich in Parieren sehr schlecht bin gelingt mir es in diesem Spiel überraschend gut. Das Gameplay funktioniert recht gut ohne Fehler (bis jetzt), die Story ist auch gut geschrieben, und die Musik ist auch Toll. Im Grossen und ganzen ist es ein Tolles spiel, es darf aber ruhig etwas Schwerer sein.

user_reviews.author: joaonogarau
user_reviews.quote: After a 20-year wait, I have to say my feelings about playing Onimusha again are mixed.There are nostalgic touches here and there. The Genma clearly draw inspiration from the classic Onimusha titles. Kyoto brings to mind the market setting from Onimusha 2. It feels as though Jubei or Samanosuke might show up at any moment.However, what used to be a game focused heavily on hack-and-slash action has shifted to a different style. It isn't necessarily bad, but the gameplay is completely different. If you look at Devil May Cry, for instance, you can see how faithful it remained to the gameplay style of its **** short: After 20 years, what I really wanted was a sequel to those wonderful games that defined my childhood—seeing a new hero like Jubei Yagyu save the day. Instead, the sequel introduced a combat system that feels alien compared to the original, creating a steep learning curve for those unfamiliar with this particular **** knows? Maybe one day they’ll release a true new Onimusha game that stays faithful to the classics.

user_reviews.author: Javier444
user_reviews.quote: Como fan desde pequeño de los onimusha la verdad me he llevado una pequeña decepcion, los enemigos son lentos, los jefes demasiado faciles, es un juego centrado en jugadores casuales. Se convierte demasiado rapido en un juego repetitivo y añadirle ese medio “mundo abierto” de Kyoto no hace mas que restarle, no he llegado ni a mitad del juego y me parece que capcom aqui ha chirriado un poco, no es fiel a los onimushas y mucho menos a un soulslike, es una pena pero no lo recomiendo a no ser que te gusten los juegos de pulsar botones y brillos bonitos, por lo demas, ni lo compres, 80 euros que la verdad dejan mucho que desear hasta en las animaciones y gestos de personajes principales, parece de ps3 en algunos momentos.

user_reviews.author: ChatGamer
user_reviews.quote: Il y a aucune difficulté, les soins sont infinies avec des herbes qui heal tout les deux mètres. Les ennemies n'attaquent pas, et les Boss foutent aucune pression. Ce jeu est un jeu exclusivement pour casual gamer rien de plus.
